PySpark is easiest to learn by connecting it to concepts you already know from pandas and SQL—then noticing where distributed execution changes the rules.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key ideas
`SparkSession` `schema` `select` `filter` `withColumn`
`groupBy` `join` `window` `partition` `Parquet` `explain`
:::

## A small PySpark pipeline

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

df = spark.read.parquet("events/")

result = (
    df.filter(F.col("event") == "purchase")
      .groupBy("country")
      .agg(
          F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"),
          F.count("*").alias("orders")
      )
)

result.show()
```

The syntax is not the hard part. The important question is:

> **What physical work will Spark need to perform?**

## Learn in this order

```text
DataFrame basics
 ↓
schemas + data types
 ↓
select/filter/withColumn
 ↓
groupBy
 ↓
joins
 ↓
window functions
 ↓
read/write Parquet
 ↓
partitions + shuffle
 ↓
query plans
 ↓
performance
```

## pandas vs. Spark

```text
pandas
DataFrame → usually local/in-memory

Spark
DataFrame → logical distributed dataset
          → optimized plan
          → tasks over partitions
```

Avoid Python UDFs when equivalent built-in Spark expressions exist; built-in expressions give Spark more opportunity to optimize execution.

## DS/ML bridge

A common architecture is:

```text
raw distributed data
       ↓
Spark cleaning / aggregation / features
       ↓
training dataset
       ↓
ML training
       ↓
batch/stream scoring pipeline
```

Spark is often the **data engineering layer around ML**, not necessarily the algorithm that trains every model.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Best debugging habit
When a Spark job is surprisingly slow, do not only stare at Python code. Inspect the execution plan, partitions, joins, shuffles and data volume.
:::
